title: Trump Mocked a Fox News Reporter's Fiancé - Hours Later It Blew Up in His Face
text:
1 days ago Donald Trump’s habit of publicly humiliating anyone who strays even slightly from MAGA orthodoxy appears to have backfired yet again, this time with a Republican congressman now openly threatening to sabotage one of the administration’s most controversial billion-dollar deals after Trump decided to take a bizarre swipe at the lawmaker through his Fox News fiancée.
The drama erupted Wednesday after Fox News correspondent Jacqui Heinrich attempted to ask Trump whether he had spoken with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Instead of answering the question, Trump abruptly launched into a rambling complaint about Heinrich’s fiancé, Republican Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania.

“Well, her husband votes against me all the time. Can you imagine?” Trump said while addressing other reporters.
Trump then continued spiraling into a personal grievance session.
“I don’t know what’s with him. You better ask what’s with him. Her husband, she’s married to a certain congressman. He likes voting against Trump. You know what happens with that? Doesn’t work out well. I don’t know why he does.”
The exchange was awkward for multiple reasons — not least because Trump appeared confused about Heinrich and Fitzpatrick’s relationship status. While the president repeatedly referred to Fitzpatrick as Heinrich’s husband, Fox News reportedly clarified that the two are still engaged.
But the real problem for Trump came later. Within hours, Fitzpatrick, one of the few remaining Republicans representing a genuinely competitive swing district, publicly declared war on Trump’s newly announced $1.776 billion “Anti-Weaponization Fund,” the controversial arrangement tied to Trump dropping his massive lawsuit against the Department of Justice.
“Bad news, we’re gonna try to kill it,” Fitzpatrick told MeidasTouch reporter Scott MacFarlane.
The fund has already generated enormous backlash because it is designed to compensate people who claim they were unfairly targeted by the federal government during the Biden administration, including January 6 defendants and other MAGA loyalists. Critics across the political spectrum have blasted the arrangement as an extraordinary abuse of executive power and a taxpayer-funded payout operation for Trump allies.
Fitzpatrick made clear he is not merely issuing a symbolic complaint.
“We’re going to write a letter to the AG to start, but we’re considering a legislative option,” he said, adding that lawmakers are still trying to determine “exactly what the legal machinations are.”
“Can’t do that,” he added bluntly.
The Pennsylvania Republican also zeroed in on one of the most explosive reported details of the agreement: provisions that allegedly shield Trump, his family, affiliated businesses, and related trusts from future IRS scrutiny. According to the report, the settlement declares the IRS is “FOREVER BARRED and PRECLUDED” from “prosecuting or pursuing” claims or examinations involving Trump and related entities.
Asked whether his effort would target those provisions too, Fitzpatrick didn’t hesitate.
“Of course, yeah, you can’t do that.”
That response matters because Fitzpatrick is not some random anti-Trump Republican relic clinging to cable-news relevance. He represents a purple Pennsylvania district Democrats have aggressively targeted for years, and he has repeatedly attempted to maintain some distance from Trumpism while still surviving inside today’s GOP.
Trump’s public habit of turning even friendly or neutral reporters into targets has increasingly created political collateral damage for Republicans already struggling in swing districts. Heinrich herself has periodically drawn MAGA backlash for fact-checking Trump or pressing the administration during White House exchanges, despite working for Fox News — a network Trump still treats as an extension of his political apparatus whenever coverage is sufficiently flattering.

Now the president appears to have managed the rare feat of insulting both a Fox News reporter and a Republican congressman in one breath — while simultaneously energizing internal GOP resistance to a legally dubious billion-dollar arrangement critics are already calling a slush fund for loyalists.
And in classic Trump fashion, it all started because somebody asked a basic foreign-policy question.
